for the group gue/ngl. let me begin by thanking in particular the rapporteur, julia girling, and the other shadow rapporteurs. i think it was not always an easy job, and i think it was a rather time-consuming job, and yet i dare say that the rapporteur in particular, as our leader, did it and did it well. however, looking back at the whole negotiation of this directive, i am a little sad because i also see it as a missed opportunity. the final text is a mere shadow of the ambitious text originally approved. the conclusion of the negotiations was negatively affected by two things. firstly, panic fear of the incoming presidency of the council and secondly, excuse me, brexit, which at that time was only a few days old from its shocking birth. in this atmosphere, we panicked unnecessarily, and the end result is to be known. the biggest problem i see is that the original text, in its pre-trialogue version, contained a legally binding commitment to reduce the health burden on people from air pollution by 52% compared to 2005. the text voted at the same time, however, agrees with the council's proposed value of 49.6%, while the red line was 50%. but behind these abstract numbers are concrete, preventable, extra lives lost. and i'm not even gonna comment on the other huge concessions we've served to the council on a silver platter. so it's very difficult for me to relate to this document. but i would like to end on a positive note. any improvement in air quality is a way forward and will help people's health, even in situations where it could have been greater. and while i see that figure as a big disappointment, ultimately, this number could mean cleaner air than our citizens are breathing right now, and that's certainly, albeit a small, positive.
i welcome the agreement on reducing national emissions of certain air pollutants, even though the resulting compromise falls short of the european parliament's ambitions. overall, the health-related emissions are to be reduced by 49,6% by 2030, which is clearly an improvement over the current situation. the proposed reduction targets were informally agreed during the dutch presidency of the eu council. the czech republic, which supports the current proposal and has already made stricter reduction commitments by 2020 than the text of the directive, agreed with them. it is also in line with the approved framework position of the czech republic and will have positive impacts on air quality both as a result of measures taken in the czech republic and as a result of reduced transboundary pollution. i would also like to stress that the proposed reduction targets are acceptable and achievable without imposing an unbearable burden on the economy. it is important to recognise that air pollution not only has negative effects on health and the environment, but also causes external costs of between eur 330 and 400 billion, including direct economic damage of eur 15 billion (absence from work due to health problems), eur 4 billion (healthcare costs), eur 3 billion (loss of crop yields) and eur 1 billion as a result of damage to buildings.
the cop 22 final declaration characterises the implementation of the current paris commitment as an urgent obligation. today, more than ever, it is necessary that developed countries re-emphasise their commitment to implement the paris agreement and ensure adequate funding, especially for developing countries. last year, we made history by bringing all the major players to the climate talks, including those who have long refused to accept their share of responsibility for the fate of the world, including the united states. but their new president has said that he is putting that success in jeopardy, and i hope very much that he will really stick to his word. president trump should realize that his stance will directly affect other major polluters. if the u.s. withdraws from the treaty, the rest of the big players will withdraw from the treaty, and with them, the rest of the world. the real danger is that europe will be left alone in its struggle. i would very much like to see this end. we must appeal to mr. trump to realize his enormous share of responsibility for the fate of the planet and to stand up to him as the man he likes to call himself.

in writing. i supported the agreement reached by the ep and the council at second reading, which sets stricter national ceilings for emissions of air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds (solvents, solvents, detergents), ammonia and fine particulate matter. the resulting agreement of a european average of national emission ceilings of 50% is a compromise between the original stricter position of the ep, which proposed a european average of national ceilings of 52%, and the more moderate position of the member states in the council, which proposed 48%. the adopted directive will contribute to improving air quality in the eu and in the czech republic its effects will be felt positively, especially by the inhabitants of border regions exposed to pollution from some neighbouring countries. air pollution knows no borders and therefore the issue of air quality must be tackled at european level.
in writing. the revision of the directive on annual emission limits for toxic air pollutants aims, in particular, to ensure further reductions in these emissions and thus to prevent health risks linked to air quality. the report was the subject of very long and complex council discussions, particularly because of pressure from countries such as the united kingdom, france, italy and poland. there have also been many changes in the attitudes of the various parliamentary groups. i am glad that our rapporteur, julia girling, has finally managed to find support across the spectrum, with the exception of the green group, for whom this report is clearly not ambitious enough. i would like to see a consensus on higher objectives, but i think that the compromise reached is the maximum possible in the present situation and i believe that it will be acceptable to the council.
in writing. i supported the european parliament's report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the reduction of national emissions of certain atmospheric pollutants and amending directive 2003/35/ec, which is at third reading. the directive sets targets for reducing emissions of the most serious air pollutants (sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds or ammonia) by setting reduction targets for 2030 for each member state and the eu as a whole against the 2005 reference values. the eu has committed to reducing its total emissions by 49.6% by 2030. although the european parliament went further in setting emission reduction targets than the commission's proposal, the czech republic has achieved achievable targets that will not impose an insurmountable economic burden. it is also important for our country to limit cross-border pollution, which comes mainly from poland. i am convinced that the targets for reducing emissions of the most serious pollutants we voted on today will contribute in the long term to reducing the negative impacts of these emissions on the environment and on people's health.
in writing. ‒ air pollution is a major health risk in the eu that causes more than 400 000 premature deaths each year. it is a cross-border threat that must be tackled at the european level. this directive will save lives: it will avoid tens of thousands of premature deaths annually and improve the quality of the environment. meeting the new targets will cut the negative health effects of pollution by half by 2030. tackling air pollution also brings economic benefits to society, since the economic cost of the health impacts of air pollution is estimated at 3-9% of gdp.

in writing. ‒ the current security environment is characterised by less predictability and, conversely, more interconnectedness of other sectoral areas linked to it. the dynamics of security threats are so sudden that it is necessary to respond more flexibly to current events. to do this, the common security and defence policy needs to have the appropriate resources and tools. i supported this report because i agree with its vision of sustained and structured cooperation between member states and an integrated approach to crises. i would also like to stress the importance of deeper cooperation in the field of cyber defence. cyberattacks can be devastating, and it is therefore essential to prepare together as best we can for this form of criminal activity.
in writing. the common security and defence policy has been one of the major topics of discussion within the community since the 1950s. the first six gradually expanded to include other advanced industrial nations, each producing its own weapons, whether handguns or other. the original concept, the western european union, was to bring about a convergence of standards and possible cooperation among arms manufacturers. especially after france's withdrawal from the nato military component and the relocation of its headquarters to brussels, the project took on a real contour. after de gaulle's retirement, it was enough to cough up a significant amount of overseas, or raise an eyebrow at the supreme head of nato, and new weapons, especially in the renewal of the air fleet and other modern systems were purchased from the usa. yet, from time to time, there is an attempt to refresh the original concept and to support the eu military-industrial complex. perhaps the only area where this has been achieved and where the eu is competing successfully is the airbus consortium, but this is mainly for civil use. only two successful multi-role implementations remain, both in the aerospace field, the eurofighter typhoon and gripen. we therefore call for the implementation of a common security and defence policy in accordance with the un charter and international law. it is necessary to separate the eu and nato in a consistent manner. weapons of mass destruction of all kinds must be banned and eliminated worldwide.

in writing. ‒ i support the report presented because i believe that the eu's common security and defence policy should be clearly strengthened. on a theoretical level, i am convinced that the creation of a common european army would be clearly beneficial and that these units could effectively support the forces of the north atlantic alliance, which currently represents our only security alternative. on the other hand, i'm a realist, and i think that the creation of a european army would actually have the same problems that nato has now. i refer in particular to the unwillingness of states to contribute to their own defence and the general unwillingness of states to deal with defence at a collective level. as a first step towards common defence, eu countries should therefore now focus primarily on maintaining a level of defence spending of 2% of gdp, but also on improving cooperation between national armed forces. the european union should be able to respond quickly and effectively to current security threats. whether it's through cooperation between states or through joint units is not really relevant at this point.

in writing. on 23 november 2016, at the plenary session of the european parliament in strasbourg, we voted to oppose the renewal of the approval of the active substance bentazone. this is one of the many battles that my colleagues and i have fought with the european commission and its consistent practice of renewing authorizations for the use of potentially dangerous substances without proper and open scientific harm assessment consulted by the expert public. this time, the european commission has proposed to renew the authorisation of this substance for a further 15 years (for glyphosate it has been granted 7), despite the fact that the uk environment agency has detected the common presence of this pesticide in surface and groundwater and that no relevant studies have yet been carried out on the carcinogenicity of benzocaine and its effects on the human endocrine system. the substance has already been shown to have a major effect on the mammalian endocrine system, for example in laboratory rats. in the absence of clear data on the safety of the substance, i followed the precautionary principle and supported this objection. i mean, i voted against the re-authorization of bentazone.
in writing. ‒ bentazone is a widely used herbicide and an important component of plant protection and agricultural production. however, i am convinced, as the opponent is, that human and animal health and effective protection of the environment must come first, since the sustainability of agricultural production depends on all of these. the criteria for endocrine disruptors are not yet clearly defined and, despite the pressure from the agricultural sector, i think that this is a reason to wait for the relevant data on which to base these criteria. the objection does not seek to challenge the scientific research to date, but asks that verified data be made available before the substance is authorised for another 15 years as a potentially toxic and reproductive toxicant. it is also about complying with existing legislation. meps have the right to object to implementing acts and previous cases have shown that, despite the fact that there is officially no influence on the european commission's procedure, political pressure can play a crucial role in the outcome.
in writing. ‒ while i consider it important to apply the precautionary principle when there is a potential danger for human or environmental health, in this case, several circumstances justify a more cautious approach, in particular against the background of the still unresolved questions over a proper definition for criteria for endocrine disruptors. for this reason but also because of the potential interest-related matter of the ano leader i decided to abstain.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, let me start by thanking the rapporteur, mr langen, and everybody who has contributed to this very significant report. we are very glad of your valuable guidance for the commission and i am also glad that we share the same views on many of these issues. vat is a big source of revenue for the member states and that is why, every once in a while, we have to check if everything in this field is fit for purpose because the world around us is changing. there are obviously some shortcomings which we have to address. first, member states are faced with a massive revenue loss. the vat gap has been estimated at around eur 160 billion each year. cross-border fraud alone accounts for eur 50 billion each year. second, complying with vat rules for cross—border and digital activities is still very cumbersome. compliance costs need to be reduced. third, we must adapt the system to technological progress, tax goods and services where they are consumed, and give member states more flexibility in setting vat rates. the commission, via the action plan, sets out immediate and urgent actions to tackle the vat gap and adapt the vat system to the digital economy, e—commerce and the needs of small and medium—sized enterprises. it provides a clear orientation towards a robust, definitive vat system for cross—border supplies and proposes options for modern and flexible rules on vat rates. overall this action plan sets out progressive steps towards a modernised and rebooted vat system tailored to the single market. the proposed initiatives are numerous and ambitious, but i believe that they are realistic with their step—by—step approach. i am pleased that the report of the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) welcomes many of these. the option we put forward for the definitive vat system based on the – already agreed – destination principle consists in taxing intra—eu supplies in the member states of destination via an extended one—stop shop. i warmly welcome parliament’s support in the report adopted by econ and its strong reference to the principle of the fractionated payments of vat, which should remain a core element of the definitive vat system. this would ensure a consistent treatment with domestic supplies and drastically reduce cross—border fraud. it has been estimated that this option would reduce cross—border vat fraud by 80%. in real terms eur 40 billion more could be collected per year. other options, like the generalised reverse charge, which econ’s report recommends, do not offer the same potential. in fact replacing vat by a sort of sales tax could significantly increase fraud and administrative burdens for businesses. in our view, this is not the right approach. the time has also come to adapt the vat rates legislation to the definitive vat system based on the destination principle, which should allow for creative rates flexibility for member states. i welcome parliament’s willingness to provide us with a clear guidance on the options we have set out in the vat action plan. we will give full consideration to this guidance when preparing our legislative proposals next year. by the end of this year the commission will already address some of your recommendations in a series of ambitious legislative proposals. as regards smes and e-commerce, the commission’s upcoming proposal will include a threshold and other simplification initiatives targeted at small and micro-businesses, including an extended and enhanced one—stop shop mechanism. this proposal will also address current distortions putting eu businesses at a significance disadvantage compared to non-eu businesses, which can legally supply small consignments vat-free into the eu annually and frequently omit paying the vat they should. as regards rates for e-publication, our upcoming proposal will give member states the option of aligning the vat treatment of e—publication, such as books, newspapers and periodicals, with that of printed publication. taking into account last may’s ecofin council conclusions on the action plan, the commission will pursue its efforts to achieve consensus. we count on parliament’s active support in this respect. the commission is equally determined to take strong actions to speed up the fight against vat fraud in the eu, an idea dear to this house. as recommended and supported by you, the commission is working to improve the administrative cooperation between the member states, in particular by reinforcing eurofisc, by more efficient and real time sharing of information, and by adding a common risk analysis, as well as by deepening cooperation with other european and national law enforcement authorities. i look looking forward to a good debate and good cooperation when trying to find good and concrete proposals next year.

the author. the case of ildar dadin for me symbolizes 3 fundamental issues of today's russia: the flagrant trampling on the right to peaceful assembly, the alarming state of the judiciary and imprisonment, including inhumane treatment and torture, the cases of those who have been arrested on false or unfounded charges or for exercising their right to freedom of expression and assembly. ildar dadin is the first citizen of the russian federation to be deprived of liberty on the basis of the scandalous article 212.1 of the criminal code, which was adopted by the russian duma in 2014. it's an article that can put anyone in jail for up to 5 years for participating in a peaceful public protest, even for peacefully holding a protest poster in public. this article so flagrantly violates the very constitution of the russian federation. if he continues to pay, he could unleash an avalanche of repression against dissenters. the case of ildar dadin thus becomes a new symbol of the trampling of human rights in russia.
the russian federation is a state that does not respect international law and does not respect its own law or regulates its own law as if it were not a law but only a tool empowering state bodies to arbitrarily treat its own citizens. i myself have lived under a totalitarian regime, under russian rule, so i know what i'm talking about. the case of ildar dadin and other political prisoners who are imprisoned and tortured for daring to speak their minds freely is proof of this. a state that in the 21st century systematically tortures its own citizens in this way, while being a member of the council of europe and a signatory to the convention for the protection of human rights, is not a trusted partner in international relations and the eu should make it clear to it.
ildar dadin was standing on the sidewalk holding a banner. i don't know what he could have done against russian law, when article 31 of the russian constitution says: citizens have the right to peacefully assemble without weapons, to hold meetings, meetings and demonstrations, marches. according to article 29 (1) of the russian constitution, everyone must be guaranteed freedom of thought and expression. according to paragraph 4, everyone has the right to freely seek and receive, produce, disseminate information by any lawful means. i really don't see how mr. dadin can be kept in prison in this situation. i am very pleased that the council of europe and its court have taken this case as one of their priorities and will be dealing with it. we should find some link with the committee of ministers of the council of europe within our eu policies, so that their decisions are also respected by russia.

in writing. in the european parliament today, i voted in favour of the european parliament's motion for a resolution on the eu's accession to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. the eu should support member states in their efforts and measures to combat violence against women. the number of cases of sexual and domestic violence, which mainly affect women, is not decreasing in the eu. i therefore welcome the legislative guarantees to combat violence against women provided for by the istanbul convention and the associated commitment to take practical measures. i have some reservations about the terminology that is fixed by this convention and further allows its use for so-called gender ideology. i understand gender equality as equality between women and men and in this sense i support those measures that fulfil this concept. i think we should fight against all violence, against violence against children, including unborn children, against the elderly, in short, all violence is evil. i therefore voted against the part of the resolution which calls for the definition of violence against women as a crime at european union level and for this substance to be incorporated into the tfeu with the possibility of legislation in this area. i consider such measures to be an unnecessary and disproportionate extension of the powers of the european union, since the istanbul convention itself is already a sufficient guarantee.
in writing. i voted in favour of a resolution calling for the eu to accede to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. it is a council of europe convention covering all forms of violence, including psychological violence. the so-called istanbul convention is a key and the first legally binding international document that provides a legal framework for the contracting states. the goal of the documentary is zero tolerance for violence against women. the convention establishes definitions of related offences and calls for their criminalisation. it lays down sanctions for perpetrators and measures to prevent violence and to help victims. the czech republic is a signatory to the convention but has not yet ratified it, along with many other european countries. i hope that changes soon. in the czech republic alone, according to a 2014 survey by the eu agency for human rights, 32% of women aged 15 and over have experienced physical or sexual violence. at eu level, it was 22%, but that's not a very good result compared to 30% worldwide. i therefore commend the efforts of the ep and the commission, led by commissioner jourová, to get the convention accepted by the eu as a whole. the fight against violence against women should be a common theme. i believe that by working together and committing to common standards in this area, we could make tangible progress.
in writing. ‒ the eu’s accession to the istanbul convention will reinforce the eu’s commitment to combating violence against women, reinforce its credibility and accountability toward its international partners, and consolidate the eu’s actions targeting violence against women through a coordinated international effort with the exchange of data and documentation among signatory states. i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on eu accession to the istanbul convention because i believe the eu must do everything in its power to promote and better the combat against violence against women, both within the eu, as well as in third countries.
‒ i consider violence against women to be a serious crime and one of the pressing problems of our society. violence against women is often overlooked, and it is therefore our duty to raise awareness of the problem, to focus on prevention and to fight stereotypes. i therefore support the european union's accession to the istanbul convention, which requires signatories to improve the system of protection for victims of violence, to ensure the prosecution of perpetrators or, for example, to provide extended psychological assistance. in addition, the convention should also improve the system of collecting information on different instances of violence, which will help to better understand and combat this phenomenon.

‒ the european ombudsman is the body to which any citizen of the union can turn if he or she has a complaint concerning maladministration by the institutions, bodies, offices or agencies of the european union. it acts essentially as a bridge between citizens and institutions, which are often reluctant to interact with it in solving its problems. as this is a major contribution to increasing the transparency of a very complex administrative system, i voted in favour of the annual report of this body. emily o'reilly, who heads the institute, has worked to improve the quality of strategic research needed to improve the current situation. i personally welcome the ombudsman's efforts to address the issue of the non-public composition of the commission's expert groups and the pressure to publish in detail information on meetings with lobbyists. i am also pleased that the ombudsman is also investigating cases where former commission officials move to the private sector. the institution of the european ombudsman increases the opportunities for ordinary citizens to have a say in eu policy-making. this is extremely important at a time when more and more people are moving away from the european union and when we sometimes see a similar trend in the institutions themselves. the link between european structures and citizens must be restored. they're the ones who are here first.

in writing. ‒ i fully support the report on the protection of personal information relating to criminal offences between the eu and the us because i am convinced there is need to have a sort of ‘umbrella’ over all the data protection clauses included in all the eu-us agreements to date. also, and i find personally very important, the agreement brings the possibility for the citizens to seek judicial redress in case there is a breach in data protection by one of the parties concerned. finally, i welcome that public independent oversight bodies which will ensure the data protection rules are respected are part of the agreement.
in writing. ‒ the umbrella agreement establishes a framework of data protection principles and safeguards in case of transfers of personal information for criminal law purposes between the us and the eu and its member states. it would supplement the data protection provisions in existing instruments such as bilateral agreements as mutual legal assistance in criminal matters treaty, agreement on enhancing cooperation in preventing and combating serious crime and terrorist screening information agreement/arrangement as well as the eu-us pnr agreement and eu-us tftp agreement. the umbrella agreement provides a high level of personal data protection and that is why i voted in favour of it. i see it as an absolute necessity to consent to this umbrella agreement now. if we have agreements such as pnr where the transfer of data forms an integral part, we must have sufficient provisions to underpin how and when that data is transferred between the us and the eu.
‒ i consider the transfer and receipt of personal data to be a very complex subject, where the right balance must be found between security and the rights of the individual. i believe that the eu-us agreement on the protection of personal information relating to criminal offences is an example of how to preserve the rights of individuals as much as possible without compromising security. i would like to emphasise that the agreement only regulates the treatment of personal data that states already obtain under existing agreements, and does not therefore broaden the scope of the information shared. this agreement guarantees a high level of individual freedoms without compromising security. it shall clearly state how personal data must be handled in order to prevent misuse. it also gives citizens the opportunity to seek judicial redress in the event of wrongdoing, which i personally consider very important. this agreement does not regulate the exchange of data between national authorities, as these are outside the eu's remit.

in writing. in the plenary session of 1 december i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the situation in italy following the earthquakes. between august and october 2016, three devastating earthquakes struck the central apennines, killing 290 people, injuring more than 400 and displacing tens of thousands. the last of these earthquakes, on october 30, was the strongest recorded in italy since 1980. the series of earthquakes and the devastation they have caused have had a severe economic impact. it is therefore necessary to coordinate properly the sustainable regeneration of the areas in order to recover the economic and social losses caused. this proposal will allow for accelerated financing at the highest level from european union funds and the necessary assistance to the italian authorities to help ensure decent living conditions for those who have lost their homes. prevention should be an increasingly important phase of disaster management and its social importance should increase.
in writing. in a short span of less than three months, italy was struck by three devastating earthquakes, which left hundreds dead and injured, tens of thousands displaced, and vast amounts of property damaged. we must remember that the european union solidarity fund only contributes to the expenses related to the follow-up and emergency situation and that member states at risk of natural disasters must also spend large amounts on preventive measures. i therefore supported the request that the commission draw up a proposal to amend the relevant rules so that member states' expenditure on investments in reconstruction and earthquake prevention measures is not subject to union restrictions, for example so that tax benefits granted by member states to citizens affected by a disaster are not considered to be public support.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution as i believe there is a case for a more transparent, more efficient and better way to ensure independence of commissioners and limit their potential conflicts of interests. as some recent cases show, there are occasions where former commissioners can switch careers respecting fully the current code of conduct, raising at the same time some serious ethical concerns. that worries me, as it also undermines the eu’s credibility in the eyes of its citizens. we need to see this problem not only from a purely legal point of view, but to take into account a broader perspective, and that is why i think that the code of conduct as it stands now should be revised.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because i strongly support transparency in the european union institutions and i believe that the european commission and its commissioners should lead by example. the report aims to facilitate a reform of the procedures relating to commissioners’ declaration of interest to assure the maximum accountability and transparency of a commissioner’s fully independent performance of his/her mandate. it defines conflict of interest and promotes reform of the code of conduct for commissioners from 2011 to extend the post-office employment restriction to two years.
in writing. i supported the report, which responds, inter alia, to the finding that the current code of conduct for members of the commission does not adequately codify the requirement under article 245 tfeu that members of the commission observe the duty to behave with integrity and discretion when accepting certain appointments or benefits after their term of office, both during and after their term of office. it is unacceptable that the commission does not regularly report on the implementation of the code of conduct for members of the commission, in particular as regards their declarations of interests. it is appropriate to consider revising the code of conduct in order to provide for the possibility of complaints or sanctions in the event of serious misconduct within the meaning of articles 245 and 247 tfeu.
in writing. ‒ several current cases, such as the case of former european commission president barroso, have shown us how important it is that senior european officials do not get into a conflict of interest. i am therefore pleased that the committee on legal affairs is now tasked with a thorough review of the property relations of the candidates for european commissioners and with recommending that the commissioners negotiate a remedy by proposing the termination of the problematic property relations. it is also good that the property relations will be controlled during the execution of the mandate, thus avoiding further potential conflicts of interest. the committees responsible should also deal much more closely with property issues in the context of hearings of commissioners-designate. i am also pleased that the juri parliamentary committee will now have the power to decide in serious cases that a candidate cannot be a european commissioner if he or she cannot meet the requirements of the code of conduct.
in writing. ‒ i am voting for the report as a whole, but i have some doubts. i fully agree that the legal affairs committee is the body that should assess the existence of a potential conflict of interest and then also formulate recommendations for its elimination. however, i do not think that this committee is competent to assess whether the information submitted by the commissioner-designate is true or not. the extent to which the conflict of interest should be limited and how it should be understood in relation to the entrusted portfolio is also open to debate. the problems of interpreting the little detail in the provisions on the assessment of the financial interests of commissioners have been problematic, for example, during the last appointment of the european commission, and i therefore believe that this statement will help to clarify the whole situation and thus allow a better assessment of the commissioner candidates.
in writing. seas and oceans are considered an important element of the earth's ecological stability. sadly, in recent years many places have become garbage dumps. tens of tonnes of plastic are carried by rivers around the world every year, and ocean currents concentrate these 'treasures' on large floating islands. reports say that the area of the garbage island in the atlantic ocean is about the size of france. as the interests of gas and oil producers shift from land to sea, the likelihood of their facilities crashing increases. in the far north, in particular, the effects of such an accident are felt for a long time in nature. in the south, nature 'helps' to deal with the disaster much more quickly, but the losses from tourism are even worse for the surrounding countries. in both cases, the fishing industry is affected very significantly. it is good that the european commission is trying to harmonise the approach to liability for damage caused. only by coordinating legislation in the field to the maximum extent possible, ideally by introducing a globally applicable standard, can significant progress be made. the report rightly calls on the commission to carry out the necessary studies and data collection and calls on the member states to cooperate. for the reasons stated above, i welcome and support the report.
in writing. ‒ at the plenary session on 1 december, i voted in favour of the report on liability, compensation and financial security for offshore oil and gas activities. more than 90% of oil and 60% of natural gas extracted in europe comes from offshore activities. they are currently taking place or are planned in the territorial waters of 18 member states. offshore oil and gas operations are conducted in increasingly extreme conditions and therefore additional measures are needed to effectively guarantee safety before an accident occurs that would have serious and devastating consequences for the environment and the economy of marine and coastal areas. further harmonised eu-level rules on liability, compensation and financial security have prevented future accidents on the basis of the precautionary and preventive principles, as well as the 'polluter pays' principle and the principles of sustainability.
offshore oil and gas exploration and production is increasingly taking place in extreme conditions and locations and can have significant to devastating impacts on marine ecosystems, the environment and the economies of maritime areas. it's a very sensitive subject, given the enormous power of the mining industry. i was therefore pleased to support the report which calls for the independence of the competent authorities in the member states to be guaranteed and which calls on the commission to establish uniform rules for determining liability, financial security and possible compensation. so far, these rules vary quite considerably between member states, and i think that is why it is necessary to create a uniform european framework based on the models of the most advanced countries. the definition of criminal offences and penalties for infringements of safety rules in coastal waters should, of course, be harmonised.

in writing. deep-sea fishing is another of the huge environmental problems associated with the rate at which humanity is depleting natural resources. human encroachment on ecosystems is resulting in an unprecedented loss of biodiversity and loss of ecosystem services that are vital to us as human beings. in the last few decades, the intensity of deep-sea fishing has increased exponentially, a technique called bottom trawling, where fishing vessels drag nets along the bottom of the sea, often the size of a football field, turning the seabed into a virtual desert. deep-sea ecosystems have a vital impact on life in the sea and thus on the planet, and their unchecked plundering may very soon have dire consequences. i am therefore pleased that after lengthy negotiations parliament and the council have managed to reach agreement on this proposal, which aims to reduce the destructive effects of fishing in international waters in the north-east atlantic by defining a specific area in which deep-sea fishing will take place. the agreement also sets a limit of 800 metres for the depths at which fishing is permitted and proposes sanctions for vessels that violate the deep-sea fishing regulations. some vessels will also be obliged to take on board scientific observers to continue collecting data and researching the effectiveness of the regulation, which i personally consider very important.

mr president, it is a fact that human rights, as they are established by the regulations and the law of the european union, should be the subject of a debate which will take place on the floor of the european parliament. we should not become an exporter of basic human rights to all the surrounding countries, surrounding countries outside the european union. we should really be having this discussion on our own turf. i have come to the conclusion that the report as a whole is adequate, it is well written, although it does indeed fall short on some points. it is important to me that the agenda of these fundamental human rights is also integrated into our international policy. to not support regimes that undoubtedly violate the basic human rights that we recognize, whether it is the right to life, the right to respect for family privacy or the right to dignity. unfortunately, that doesn't happen very often. we shouldn't lecture the world, but we should insist on basic human rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution. it gives us a clear picture on the situation regarding the eu’s fundamental values – rule of law, human rights and democracy. i am personally glad that the resolution pays special attention to such key issues as violence against women, protection of children and rights for people with disabilities. we definitely should not lose these from our radar. finally, i would like to highlight one part which is gaining in importance: it is on digital rights. access to digital services together with privacy has become a challenge in recent years and we should reflect it properly.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it takes into consideration recent developments concerning fundamental rights in several eu member states. the current situation calls for a strong message that fundamental rights have to be protected and preserved. i am glad that it stresses the importance of full respect for the principle of subsidiarity and proportionality applying both to member states and to the eu’s institutions based on a gradual approach, including both a preventative and corrective arm. furthermore, i welcomed the special attention paid to children’s rights stressing the importance of the need for their highest protection. i find it crucial that the european union does not forget that it has been built on respect for the rule of law and that it cannot take this cornerstone for granted.
in writing. ‒ i was sorry to have had to abstain from voting on the state of fundamental rights in the eu in 2015, but i did not think that this document addressed the issue of human rights in a comprehensive way. i don't agree with the narrow interpretation of human rights that has been given lately. why is there not so much talk about them in terms of the conditions and salaries of cashiers in supermarkets or maybe mail order companies? why is the term human rights so rarely used in the context of children whose parents cannot afford to pay for their school lunches? moreover, the amendment failed to pass, stating that it condemns the fact that the economic crisis and the austerity measures taken to deal with it have seriously undermined fundamental social, civil and labour rights, including the right to access to basic needs such as education, housing, health care and social security, and have also had a negative impact on the general health of the population in some member states; calls on the eu institutions and the member states to carry out ex-ante assessments of the impact on fundamental human rights of all policies and to ensure that sufficient resources are available to ensure respect for fundamental rights and to ensure the necessary minimum level of civil, economic, cultural and social rights, with particular emphasis on the most vulnerable and socially disadvantaged groups;
in writing. i voted against. i do not agree with the call for member states to legalize civil partnerships or marriages for lgbt people. marriage legislation is a matter for the individual member states and the eu should not be pushing this kind of legislation by the member states.
in writing. ‒ today we discussed a report assessing the state of human rights in the eu in 2015. in fact, the entire content of the book is related to the topic of migration and refugees. the report analyses in detail the deplorable phenomenon of trafficking in human beings, calls for the need to ensure access to quality medical care for migrants, their integration and social inclusion, improve asylum procedures and ensure the protection of women and girls in particular from all forms of violence. of course, family reunification is another of the necessities. however, it lacks any reflection on the causes of mass migration and suggestions for long-term solutions, certainly not calls for member states to support positive campaigns explaining the need to integrate incoming refugees. that's why i abstained on the final vote.
in writing. the fight against discrimination and inequality among europeans should be one of the fundamental pillars of the function of every member of the european parliament. i supported the 2015 state of fundamental rights report because it makes it clear to the european commission that a new agenda needs to be put forward. an agenda that involves all relevant actors and representatives of citizens' rights and that, taking into account the competences of the member states of the union, is capable of ensuring equal opportunities and rights for all. it is hard to imagine that, for example, human trafficking and exploitation still exist in europe, i.e. illegal activities that are unfortunately now even more fuelled by the new communication technologies. i therefore supported the call for the european union and its member states to ratify the council of europe convention on action against trafficking in human beings and to support the work of european agencies in this field. member states are currently experiencing a growing trend of racism and xenophobia. i therefore voted in favour of a provision to ensure that measures to promote equality between citizens are incorporated as far as possible into national policies. i would very much like to see member states and their lower-level bodies promote human rights education and culture. education is a very effective means of preventing racism and intolerance. it needs to be used to its fullest potential.
in writing. i voted against the report on the state of fundamental rights in the european union in 2015. i agree that the protection of human rights and freedoms in the eu is the highest in the world, which cannot be considered a permanent state of affairs, and that the protection of human rights and freedoms must be pursued on a daily basis. i consider the eu's accession to the istanbul convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence to be an important step, although i do not think that the eu should propose any new legislation on this basis. i also welcome the fact that the report addresses the issue of migration and the social inclusion and integration of migrants, including the problem of hateful and xenophobic attitudes towards refugees. the report also recognises the link between women's sexual and reproductive health and a range of human rights; however, i cannot agree with the wording of those provisions that we must respect and protect in the same way the right of all women and girls to sexual and reproductive health and include abortion as a vital basic sexual and reproductive health service. for these reasons, i could not support the text of the report.
in writing. ‒ the annual report on the situation of fundamental rights in the eu in 2015 outlines the issues and progress made in the enforcement of fundamental rights within the eu for 2015. the report covers a wide range of rights-related topics, such as, inter alia, the protection of fundamental rights and dignity, rule of law, women’s rights and violence against women, and lgbt rights. i voted in favour of this report because i believe it is a crucial eu priority and necessity to follow up on the state of play of fundamental rights in the eu, and this cannot be successfully achieved without an appropriate assessment of such initiatives.
‒ fundamental rights are the building blocks of the european union. their active enforcement is an essential element in achieving freedom, security and democracy. the past year has been quite successful in this area in my view, and we can see some concrete examples of the eu's efforts to strengthen citizens' fundamental rights. i am referring to new rules on procedural guarantees in criminal proceedings or the completion of data protection reform. it is essential that we continue to come up with new initiatives and work to ensure that every european citizen has equal access to his or her fundamental rights. i could not vote for this report, however, because there are many points which go against my political convictions. at the same time, i believe that the report goes beyond the eu's competence.
mr president, i would also like to follow the lead of my colleague in supporting copyright protection, which is very consistently and in many paragraphs in this report. for me, copyright protection is really the most important policy for intellectual property protection, because it brings investment, innovation in the field, it also means job development, the connection with employment is absolutely obvious. i am very pleased that the 2014 directive has already brought about a more balanced understanding of the relationship between author and user, that it has brought about more transparency, but also competition between collective management organisations. i think that's very important. we would also need cultural policy, the promotion of cultural goods, to be linked to cohesion policy. unfortunately, this is not the case due to some imperfections in the general regulation. i think it is a big task for the next two and a half years to be able to change the current regulation setting for the use of aid in cohesion policy.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report because it calls for further development of a comprehensive, coherent and long-term industrial policy framework for the cultural and creative sector (ccs) in terms of growth. i believe that the eu is in a strategic position to trigger innovative spillovers in other industrial sectors, such as tourism, retail, and digital technologies and that it can take a leading role in promoting the positive impact that the creative sectors have across europe.
in writing. i voted against. i do not agree with the call for the commission to draw up a framework for cultural policy. culture is supposed to be a matter for the member states and for the individual citizen. i do not agree with the idea of involving the european investment bank in subsidising culture.
in writing. ‒ today we voted on a report on a coherent eu policy for the cultural and creative sectors. i agree that these are important sectors, which generate almost 39% of the union's gdp and employment in this sector is constantly increasing, so it is necessary to support this sector, which creates incentives for innovation. however, i believe that the report does not adequately reflect the need for copyright reform to ensure a balanced approach between the industry and consumer and producer groups, incentives for smes, etc. i also disagree that there should be increased funding for this sector, through the efsi and other funds, at a time when the eu has much more pressing problems to solve. that's why i abstained in the final vote.
in writing. i supported the report highlighting the importance of the cultural and creative sectors, which is the last sector to lack a framework strategy at eu level. the commission and the member states should establish 'study labs', creative centres, co-operation spaces, networking programmes and cultural and creative clusters and networks to promote interaction between micro, small, medium and large enterprises and between non-profit organisations and commercial companies within the cultural and creative sectors, traditional crafts, cultural heritage organisations, tourism, research centres, universities and investors. at the same time, it is essential that the eu and its member states retain the ability to protect and develop their cultural and audiovisual policies within the framework of their existing legislation, standards and agreements, including the unesco convention on the protection and promotion of the diversity of cultural expressions.
in writing. ‒ i believe that the cultural and creative sectors need to be supported in europe, as they are our common heritage. i am therefore pleased to have been able to support the resolution, which focuses on several measures to realise the full potential of this activity through the concrete definition of cultural and creative sectors. it highlights the importance of education, skills and training, its ability to create value from intellectual property, and suggests solutions to facilitate access to eu funding. i am pleased that this resolution also calls on the member states to create a legal and institutional framework for creative artistic activity in line with european standards.
in writing. ‒ cultural and creative industries (ccis) are, at the dawn of the 21st century, undergoing considerable change as a result of increased digital technologies, the economic crisis of the past several years, and considerable changes in the regulatory framework. it is therefore necessary to reflect those changes in eu policy-making and legislation. i agree with the need to focus on creative industries and their position in this dynamic environment. however, i do not agree with the extremely broad scope of the report which is in my opinion rather diluting the overall target. ccis have different specifics than other ‘traditional’ industries, but the same regulatory framework has to apply in both cases. therefore, i decided to support a number of deletions within this report and i voted in favour of the final text.
in writing. ‒ the increasing impact of globalisation and digitalisation is having an increasing impact on the traditional cultural and creative sectors. the traditional sectors are based on the talents, skills and values of the european peoples. i believe that these skills need to be preserved, as well as cultural and linguistic diversity. to achieve this, we need to adapt to the current conditions and start to connect culture and the creative sectors with modern technologies and other sectors of the current economy. i therefore vote in favour of this report because i believe that we need a coherent policy at eu level to deal with this area in the long term.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution as i believe we need to pay attention to women’s rights in the countries in our neighbourhood, countries with which we cooperate quite closely. i am also worried about the concerns raised in the text and would call on the countries to focus more on women’s issues. i would like to point out one issue here. although i am convinced there is a case for having women participating more in political and economic life, it should not be pushed, as the resolution suggests, through instruments such as obligatory quotas.
in writing. i decided to support the report on women's rights in the eastern partnership countries. while i believe that the eastern partnership countries already have so much important work ahead of them, i am convinced that the situation of women's rights in the eastern partnership countries needs to be improved, especially in the context of deep economic changes and economic uncertainty that have had a negative impact on the economic situation of women and have led to gaps in their de facto equality. in doing so, i condemn the use of sexual violence against women and girls as weapons of war, including mass rape, sexual slavery, prostitution, gender-based persecution including trafficking in human beings, as well as sex tourism, and i stress the need to combat forced marriage as defined by the united nations, including child/early marriage, and i call on the eastern neighbourhood to firmly oppose any form of exploitation and abuse of women through surrogacy.
i do not agree with the call for eastern european countries to introduce quotas for women on the electoral rolls, nor do i agree with the call for special support programmes for politicians and activists. i also do not agree that the eu budget should be used to subsidize women's organisations in eastern european countries at the expense of our taxpayers.
in writing. ‒ today we voted on a report on the evaluation of women's rights in the eastern partnership countries. all the eastern partnership countries have ratified most of the important international conventions in this area, but unfortunately women in the eastern partnership countries continue to suffer from social discrimination. there is neither equal access to employment nor equal pay for equal work between the sexes. the report explicitly refers in particular to the situation in ukraine, where more than 1.5 million people have been forcibly displaced since the beginning of the conflict, of whom two thirds are women and children, who suffer from poor access to healthcare, housing and employment. i agree that it is necessary to combat the phenomenon of trafficking in human beings, violence against women, and in particular to promote access to education and services in the field of reproductive and sexual health. that is why i supported the report.
in writing. ‒ we must recognise that the eu needs to impose gender equality and gender mainstreaming more actively through the many useful instruments of its neighbourhood policy. even though women’s rights and gender equality are included within the constitutions and legal systems of all six eastern partnership countries of armenia, azerbaijan, belarus, georgia, moldova and ukraine, social and economic discrimination and gender stereotypes remain prevalent, preventing greater inclusion of women in the labour market and participation in political decision-making processes. unfortunately, the discrimination and stereotypes also lead to violence against women and lack of sexual and reproductive health and rights. i am proud that the s&d group worked together amongst others groups who managed to improve the very general draft by tabling amendments on: lgbti persons’ rights; need for stronger involvement of women in economic decision making; access to micro-credits; the need for a change in stereotypes; support for equal sharing of unpaid work between men and women; the fight against forced (child) marriage; and combating violence against women. although the six eastern partnership countries guarantee equality between women and men, de facto inequality persists in the areas the report highlights, stressing the importance of increased pressure towards gender equality and gender mainstreaming.
in writing. the european parliament's resolution on women's rights in the eastern partnership countries addresses the same problems we are dealing with in the european union, but on a completely different level. women in these eastern partnership countries face much greater problems of economic dependency, unemployment, discrimination, lack of education and, possibly, problems in reconciling family and professional life. the main objective is to improve the political and economic situation in these countries. it is women who are often involved in civil society and are effectively helping to bring about the necessary reforms. the report rightly emphasises the need for greater involvement of women in transformation processes. where this involvement has taken place, the results have been very positive, such as in moldova, the undp project 'women in politics' mentioned in the report. despite all the advantages of this resolution, i did not end up supporting it because i do not agree that the ep, through these parliamentary resolutions, calls on member states or third countries to make reproductive and sexual health services more accessible, which means, first of all, a liberal approach to abortion.
in writing. ‒ the report on the rights of women in eastern partnership states (eap) highlights the situation in the area of women’s rights in the eap countries and points to the necessity for improvement. particularly, the report highlights the profound economic changes and economic uncertainty that have had a negative effect on the economic situation of women, leading to the regression of female equality in these countries. i voted in favour of the report, which calls on the eap countries to take immediate action to increase equality between women and men in society, including the adoption of national action plans and cooperation with international organisations and civil society stakeholders. the eu has the obligation to promote and enforce gender equality norms and women’s rights in its partner states, and i believe this report reinforces this objective.

the president-in-office of the council. as i said in july, europeans now take for granted the benefits of european integration, such as peace, passport-free travel, the ability to pay in a single currency and the choice of the country in which they want to live and work. what is worse, many in europe believe that this absolute self-evidence would exist without the european union. and even that we could be much better off without the european union. let's face it, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is in the worst crisis since its inception. but this is not a crisis of external threat, it is a crisis from within, expressed above all by the mistrust of the people and the loss of authority of the european elites. the debate on the future of the union has taken a fundamental turn this year. ask a european if he knows which country should be the next to join the european union. he'll tell you he doesn't know, but he knows very well which country should leave the european union. nowhere in the world, ladies and gentlemen, is there a group of countries that even remotely resembles the european union. we all took the hard way. on the one hand, we respect a number of national specificities. we have retained our own national identities, but at the same time we have transferred many of our key powers to a common administration. today we have a duty to return to the roots. to ask ourselves whose powers and why the nation states have given up in favour of the whole, and whether we are not making the mistake today of turning away from these roots and paying attention to issues that are secondary, irrelevant and divide europe instead of uniting it in a common interest. with a unique project, ladies and gentlemen, that doesn't exist anywhere in the world, we are gambling today with a criminal mind. to stop this gamble, let's talk about where our roots are. they're in economic cooperation, they're in shared security, they're in peacekeeping. let us not, please, force people to do otherwise than these fundamental issues, because if they do not identify with them and if they do not trust them, they will turn their backs on the union for good. the slovak republic took over the presidency in july this year with the ambition to respond to the situation. the bratislava summit was a clear first step forward, as it launched a long-delayed, all-important discussion on how to make the union better, safer and more efficient. what has happened in the union and what is happening in it today? what do we expect from the union? how do we see her future? what did we fail to do, and why? and it was with these questions that we launched the so-called bratislava process on 16 september, which should culminate next march, on the occasion of the 60th anniversary of the signing of the treaties of rome. but part of the truth, ladies and gentlemen, is that we are putting the union at risk ourselves and often at risk by the domestic political agendas of the member states. for example, there are referendums that are politically motivated, but it's clear that the results have a pan-european impact, and suddenly they become something that i would call a problem for all of us. if this trend continues, the union will be preoccupied with internal politics in the member states, we will be forced to seek solutions that break the back of our heads, to compromise our own principles, all at the expense of the eu's credibility. if this continues, i am convinced that we will lack the political energy and with it the determination to tackle the fundamental problems facing the union as a whole. i want to call on the european leaders here in the european parliament to stop pursuing their domestic agenda at the expense of the european union. we all know, but we don't want to admit, that the referendum in the uk was purely an internal political agenda that politicians failed to manage. we all know that the referendum in italy was a purely domestic political agenda that was not handled. but the consequences of such decisions, for example in a possible referendum on whether or not italy should remain in the eurozone, would be absolutely disastrous for the european union and ideas. so once again, i call on european leaders to stop pursuing their domestic agenda at the expense of all of us here in europe. the current crises in the union should be seen as a good impetus to take action towards a more transparent union. the current crisis of confidence in our citizens is a good opportunity to create a clearer and more honest communication bridge between the political elites and the european public. it is alarming that according to the latest surveys, up to 57% of young europeans feel that they are marginalised and excluded from economic and social life as a result of the crisis in their country. we - the political leaders - are here to give our people not just hope, but the confidence that we can solve the crisis. that despite the unpredictability of the external environment, we have control over our own direction. we must build on the strengths of our community. the european union as a haven of peace, where peace, democracy, the rule of law, human rights, human dignity, freedom and solidarity are the fundamental and timeless pillars of our coexistence. but also the european union as a modern hub of digital progress and innovation. the european union as a conscious driver in the fight against climate change. the european union as the world's largest donor of development aid. the european union is only strong and capable of action if it is united. this was the conclusion reached at the bratislava summit. the european twenty-seven are determined to overcome and overcome the challenges of the present and the future together. but the process of reflection, as necessary as it is, is not enough on its own. without action, the most beautiful idea is worthless. the bratislava summit was therefore not just a reflection, but concrete steps towards making the european union both more understandable and a safe place for its citizens to live. and when i talk about security, i don't just mean external and internal security, the fight against terrorism, but also economic and social security, job security, income security, climate and environmental security. these are all areas of concern to union citizens. not the pun that we want to change in the european union treaties. not endless debate about whether we want more or less europe. the citizens of the european union want an economically strong european union. a union based on investments that contribute to economic growth and job creation. when i stood before you in july, i said that if we want to have such a union, we must make better use of the financial instruments available. our ambition has come true. today, thanks to the excellent cooperation between the council and the european parliament, we have a budget of the european union for 2017 that is flexible, balanced and, above all, reflects our current priorities. that's very good news. the budget adopted next year will increase resources to support economic growth and employment by 12%. we will also be better equipped to deal with migration and its causes, and to enhance the security and protection of the european union's borders. citizens also call for new investment opportunities in the union. i am therefore very pleased that the extension of the duration and financial capacity of the european fund for strategic investments has moved closer to reality. by encouraging the use of public funds, we will give the necessary impetus to private investment, which can bring new jobs. the european union citizen also wants to have a job so that he can take care of himself and his loved ones without worry. the single market is already creating many new jobs and making our daily lives easier. by completing the digital single market, we can open up a whole host of other opportunities. so i am very pleased that we have managed to make significant progress on this agenda. for example, unjustified geo-blocking may soon be a thing of the past. we'll help both the consumer and the retailer. discrimination on grounds of nationality, residence or place of business has no place in the union. in today's world, the free movement of citizens of the european union must also extend to the digital space. this also applies to the abolition of roaming charges. moreover, to realise the full potential of the single market, we need an affordable, stable and sustainable supply of clean energy. the energy union can help us achieve this. even in the final days of our presidency, we are working together to take the union further in this area. an ambitious and effective climate policy is also an integral part of the energy union. by ratifying the paris agreement, the european union has confirmed its global leadership in the fight against climate change. we also sent an important message abroad that when it comes to global challenges, we are able to take responsibility and work closely together. one of those challenges, of course, is migration. today, we know that the migration crisis is neither a seasonal nor a regional issue, but a global one. and although our views on how to deal with it sometimes differ, the citizen of the european union wants to know that we are able to offer a constructive common approach. i am glad that we have shown in the recent period that we can reach agreement here too if we want to and move this agenda forward. the european border and coast guard, which started its activities on 6 october, thanks to the swift and effective cooperation of the european parliament and the council, is a clear example. the issue of responsibility and solidarity is also closely linked to migration. i know these terms have stirred a variety of emotions in the past few months. but i believe we can all agree that each member state must not hesitate to lend a helping hand if necessary. but at the same time, i believe that we should take into account the real possibilities, capacities and capabilities of the individual member states. and i'm glad that we've shown in the last few months that we can at least talk openly about this difficult topic. this is also the case with the slovak presidency's proposal on so-called effective solidarity. i hope that this concept will be one of the elements of the mosaic in the reform of the common european asylum system. but there are other challenges. in addition to protecting the external borders, we must ensure the functionality of schengen, work closely with third countries, in particular transit countries and countries of origin of migrants, and tackle the causes of migration. and progress on the creation of a european fund for sustainable development should help. it aims in particular to address the root causes of migration by creating jobs, promoting investment and facilitating sustainable development in partner countries. ladies and gentlemen, the citizen of the european union wants to feel stability. in today's uncertain world, the union should be seen by the citizen as a basic anchor. for it to be a truly stable, secure, and prosperous place to live, we need to have good relations with neighbors as well as distant allies. and we need to be substantially more sovereign on some foreign policy issues. i'm going to ask a question that may become a reality, if for example the us administration changes its mind on sanctions against the russian federation, how do we copy this position. it's there that we'll see whether or not we're truly sovereign in these views. we also have a big problem if what the us administration is suggesting happens, and that is a very low presence, engagement in the european space. at the same time, i believe that we will continue successfully with the concrete implementation of the warsaw declaration of eu and nato leaders on strengthening mutual strategic cooperation of the two organisations. an effective enlargement policy also leads to a better resilience of the union. this is crucial to supporting the transformation and consolidating stability in south-eastern europe. to this end, new chapters have been opened in the accession process with montenegro and serbia, and there have also been positive developments in the application of bosnia and herzegovina for membership of the union. it must be in our interest that all candidate countries continue to undergo political and economic reforms that bring them closer to the union and strengthen the rule of law. free, fair and balanced trade based on reciprocity and mutual benefits is also of key importance for the internal and external stability of the union. the adoption of the free trade agreement with canada is a good example of this. this modern and ambitious agreement will not only strengthen the union's economic position, but also open up new business opportunities for our citizens. ladies and gentlemen, the only answer to the current wave of euroscepticism is to bring the meaning, substance and real achievements of the european integration project closer together through concrete results. otherwise we will open the door to different interpretations and speculations that justify anti-european politicians. in this context, we are likely to face another major challenge from next spring to ensure that the process of the united kingdom's withdrawal from the european union is transparent with the full involvement of the member states, and i would add, although these words have already been criticised on more than one occasion, that the negotiations must lead to the conclusion that it is worthwhile to remain a member state of the european union. if the negotiations prove that it is not worth being a member state of the european union, there is a risk that the negative mood in europe will grow. and we have to avoid that, because we can set an incredibly dangerous example for countries where perhaps euroscepticism is very strong. the slovak presidency has therefore made every effort to send a positive message to the european public through its work and results. so we have done our best to bring tangible results that affect the daily lives of each of us. our aim was not only to prevent further fragmentation of the union, but also to reassure our citizens that the european union is a project with a future. i want to assure you that the responsibility that we felt at in writing. ‒ today we discussed a report which, in terms of content, is part of the so-called railway package and responds to the changes that have taken place in the railway sector since 1969, when the original regulation on common rules for the standardisation of the accounts of railway undertakings was adopted. the amended legislation allows member states to reimburse railway undertakings for payments linked to obligations which other modes of transport are not required to fulfil. these include special payments in the event of accidents at work, pensions for railway employees who perform heavy work and retire early, or payments for the cost of level crossing facilities. i supported the report.
in writing. ‒ the compromise text negotiated between the european parliament and the council of the political pillar of the so-called fourth railway package is a compromise on a very sensitive subject. over the years, we have heard many arguments for and against further opening up of markets. supporters of liberalisation talk of the pressure to be more efficient in a competitive environment, while opponents argue that in the long term, liberalisation has failed to deliver better and safer services for passengers and more dignified working conditions. it's the opposite. the rules for opening up markets must therefore be clear, also with regard to quality standards and social standards for employees. cheaper is not necessarily better, and if opening up markets means precariousness and worsening conditions for employees, it would be a loss for the railway sector as a whole.
in writing. ‒ i opposed the motion for rejection because i wished to support the agreement reached on the repeal of regulation 1192/69 on the normalisation of accounts of railway undertakings. the regulation compensates railway undertakings for the payments of obligations which other modes of transport do not have to support. with the opening of the market, such measures are inconsistent with more recent eu legislation as railway undertakings continue to compete with other modes of transport but also between themselves. i therefore consider that such compensation should be managed according to the same principles applying to commercial companies. directive 2012/34/eu establishes a different framework for such compensation and should have been transposed into national law already from 2015. i hope to see the repeal of regulation 1192/69 as early as possible without a further transitional period, but in the spirit of finding a compromise, i agree to support another year of transition period.
