in writing. i voted in favour of the so-called fourth railway package, which will open up the markets for national rail passenger transport in the member states. i consider that opening up the railway market to competition is the right step to improve the quality of services provided to consumers, to reduce the cost of rail services and to improve the efficiency of public funding in this sector. the legislation also brings about the much needed separation of railway infrastructure managers from railway undertakings, which has already taken place in the czech republic several years ago. i also welcome provisions aimed at ensuring an adequate level of protection for workers in the sector, but which do not go beyond the limits of proportionality. on the contrary, i am concerned about the authorisation of existing holding companies between railway undertakings and infrastructure managers. although the infrastructure manager must act independently when awarding contracts through a tendering procedure, in the case of a holding company it will be difficult to avoid a conflict of interest or an information advantage for the entities that would form a holding company with the infrastructure manager. i see the risk in allowing railway holding companies to exist that the idea of opening up railway markets to free competition is denied.
in writing. i voted in favour of the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2012/34/eu as regards the opening of the market for national rail passenger services and the management and operation of railway infrastructure. this proposal should open the national market for rail services to international competition. czech companies will be able to penetrate foreign markets with their services. this proposal also addresses the institutional separation of rail infrastructure management from the operation of transport services. the european parliament attaches great importance to the accounting and technical separation of infrastructure and transport revenues in the case of the 'holding' model, thus ensuring a level playing field.

in writing. coal and steel were the two commodities that gave birth to the industrial revolution in the 18th century. after dramatic changes in these two industries over the last 30 years, there has been a radical reduction in coal mining and a fundamental change in steel production. the world market has been created for both commodities, and the failure rather than the success of the privatisation of the entire sector raises new questions. in any event, the use of new coal processing technologies and the introduction of new trends in steel plants is an important part of the industrial future of the developed countries of the world. the eu cannot afford to be without research and development in this area. there is always a social aspect to all activities in coal mining and processing and steel production. the impact on employment in some regions is crucial. the environmental impact is significant and emissions from steel processing and coal use are an important item in the context of eu environmental policies. in addition to the well-known chemical production, the use of co2 in agriculture and in various chemical and biochemical processes can be of great interest. it is important that the european union should also be at least in touch with the front of the troubleshooting peloton in this area of industrial activity.

in writing. today we discussed a report that addresses the research program of the research fund for coal and steel. the eu has been supporting coal and steel research for more than 50 years. the treaty establishing the european coal and steel community (ecsc) was signed in 1951. in 2002, when the treaty expired, it was decided that the assets of the esuo (and the related interest) would be released to the research fund for coal and steel (rfsc). the programme is financed by the revenues generated by the remaining assets of the (defunct) esuo. it shall be administered by the commission. the research fund for coal and steel shall complement horizon 2020 and shall be managed independently of it. it provides annual funding of around eur 50 million for research and development and innovation in the coal and steel sectors. the rapporteur took the view that the alignment of the rules of the research fund for coal and steel with those of horizon 2020 does not require a change in the legal basis, which i fully agree with, and i therefore supported the report.
in writing. ‒ the research fund for coal and steel (rfcs) was established after the expiry of the european coal and steel community treaty (ecsc) in 2012 and provides annually around 50 million euros, from the eu general budget, managed by the commission for r&d and innovation funding to the coal and steel sectors (27.2% for coal and 72.8% for steel) in order to develop knowledge and foster innovation. the proposed revision of the rfcs legal basis is focused on the management rules for the programme and is in line with the procedures and concepts used for horizon 2020, the eu programme for research and innovation, which will act as an outline for the rules for participation and dissemination in the rfcs programme. as a shadow rapporteur for this file i decided to focus mainly on issues of transparency and support for smes to be able to benefit more from this fund. all my amendments were endorsed by the ep. i did not support amendments which went beyond the framework of the programme or which would lead to a significant change to the basis for the programme, as that is not necessary in my opinion. in the final vote i supported the texts as proposed by the ep.

in writing. i supported the report by rapporteur a. delahay on the instruments of the common agricultural policy designed to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets. the resolution adopted de facto describes the current situation on agricultural markets and proposes a number of active solutions to mitigate the fluctuations in agricultural prices. i consider the provision calling on the commission to create an eu legislative framework prohibiting unfair trading practices in the food chain to be absolutely essential. following the june resolution on unfair trading practices by the rapporteur, mr e. cezsak, of the imco committee, in which i participated as shadow rapporteur, this is another of the specific calls by the european parliament to the commission, this time from the agri committee, to finally address the current imbalance of power between the various actors in the food chain.
in writing. i supported the own-initiative report on instruments to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets. farmers are often exposed to price volatility due to many factors, whether natural or economic, such as exchange rates or the prices of fertilisers and energy. the risk of price volatility can not only lead to insecurity among farmers in terms of securing their livelihood and income, but can also discourage many young start-up farmers from starting a business. it is therefore necessary to confront the volatility of agricultural prices, to look for the causes of the problem and to find appropriate solutions. the report presents some ideas that can be supported and developed further. these include, for example, the adoption of appropriate measures to support agriculture in less-favoured regions and, in particular, the strengthening of the bargaining power of producers through the creation of standardised and balanced collective agreements, which can ultimately guarantee protection against unfair trading practices by retail chains. i also welcome the consideration of the possibility of more frequent use of so-called derivatives, i.e. contracts where the price for a certain quantity of commodity is fixed, better information on eib financing programmes and the creation of a european centre for monitoring the prices of agricultural products from the producer to the final selling price.
in writing. ‒ the constant rise in agricultural prices on the world markets since the financial crisis in 2007 have resulted in price volatility in agricultural markets everywhere. as a result, price volatility has become a high priority on the international political agenda. the eu’s common agricultural policy (cap) is a set of mechanisms that were developed to help curb volatility. however, the cap tools have proven to be inefficient and therefore little used by member states. i voted in favour of the report, which asks that the cap tools be looked at and scrutinised, and additional solutions be proposed in order to render effective cap, with the aim of helping to curb volatility in agricultural markets.

in writing. on 15 december 2016, we voted in favour of a resolution in support of the survivors of the thalidomide tragedy at the european parliament plenary session in strasbourg. the thalidomide tragedy was one of the main reasons for the creation of eu pharmaceutical legislation, which has since been designed to ensure that medicines placed on the market guarantee a high standard of quality and safety to european citizens. thalidomide was used in the late 1950s and early 1960s as a medicine for morning sickness in pregnant women, as well as for headaches, insomnia and colds. this treatment has been commercially available in various european countries for several years, but only ex post has it been shown to have serious side effects, especially in pregnant women whose children were subsequently born with congenital malformations. this tragedy has affected several eu countries, whose survivors face daily serious and worsening physical consequences and indignities in reimbursing the cost of their treatment. the resolution was tabled following an oral question to the commission and a debate in plenary in march this year. i believe that the states concerned should amend their legislation to adequately compensate the victims of this tragedy while also providing them with the best possible care. that's why i voted for this resolution.
‒ the impact of thalidomide use by pregnant women on thousands of children needs to be addressed. it is completely unacceptable that the manufacturer of this substance apologized to those who have to live with the disability caused by its product only in 2012. as victims age, their health problems worsen and the cost of appropriate care increases. all those who have to live with the disability caused by thalidomide should therefore receive compensation guaranteeing a decent living conditions, regardless of the country in which they live.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the anti-morning sickness drug thalidomide. it was created in 1953 in germany by the grünenthal group. thalidomide was marketed in a number of european countries including spain, italy, germany, the uk and ireland and led to the birth of children with severe malformations. thalidomide was pulled from the market in 1961 after it was linked to birth defects but many victims have only recently received compensation. the thalidomide tragedy caused immense physical suffering and emotional hardship for the victims and their families. the drug approval regulatory framework in europe has since greatly evolved with the overarching objective being to better safeguard human health.

in writing. – a well-functioning customs code is essential to a well-functioning single market. this is not possible if member states do not respect this code or allow it to be updated to the changing situation on the ground. we need to simplify the complex customs rules and procedures which are particularly detrimental to our smes. we need to complete the digitalisation of custom controls well before the end of the transitional period to do so. for all this, we need action from the council and better controls by the member states and the commission. this is an area that is in theory already harmonised. i simply do not understand why we do not enforce it as such. our borders are only as strong as their weakest point. if a trader can cheat by going to member state a instead of member state b, he will. if a trader knows he will get a smaller fine if he is caught in member state a instead of member state b, he will go there. member states must do their jobs in a way that is standardised, no matter where you are in europe.
